https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An informational booklet from the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) covering its 2024 Board of Directors elections, included in the Troy Board of Education's February 6, 2024 workshop packet so trustees could decide how to cast the district's single ballot. It reproduces MASB bylaw provisions and profiles the candidates.

Membership framework. Under MASB Bylaws Article IV, active-member boards are grouped into eight regions defined by intermediate school district (ISD) boundaries - for example, Region 5 (Genesee, Huron, Lapeer, Sanilac, St. Clair County RESA, Tuscola), Region 7 (Eaton RESA, Hillsdale, Ingham, Jackson, Lenawee, Livingston ESA, Monroe, Washtenaw), and Region 8 (Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools, Wayne RESA), which is Troy's region. Members are also sorted into seven groups by pupil membership, from Group I (all intermediate districts) through Group VII (more than 40,000 pupils).

Board composition and rules. The MASB Board of Directors has 24 members, including three at-large directors; 16 are elected from the eight regions (two each) and one each is elected from enrollment Groups V, VI, and VII. Article VIII, Section 6 permits only one director from any single local or intermediate board, and Section 8 provides that an unopposed nominee is declared elected without an election.

Seats up in 2024. Nine seats were up (one each, three-year terms unless noted): Regions 1 (open seat), 2, 3 (one-year term), 4 (one-year term), 5, 6 (open seat), 7, 8, and Group V (one-year term). Several were settled without a ballot: Region 1 remained vacant because no nominations were received; Region 2 continues with Dawn Kaiser (Iosco RESA); Region 3 with Rick Dernberger (Zeeland Public Schools/Ottawa Area ISD); Region 4 with John Tramontana (DeWitt Public Schools); and Group V with Stephen Hyer (Clarkston Community Schools) - all unopposed.

Contested races (online balloting in Regions 5, 6, 7, and 8):
- Region 5: Janice Holz (Huron ISD, Huron County) and Roshawnda Williams (Beecher Community School District, Genesee County).
- Region 6: Robert Becker (Barry ISD), Pamela Dickinson (Comstock Public Schools, Kalamazoo County), Elizabeth O'Dell (St. Joseph County ISD), and Andrew Robinson (Berrien RESA).
- Region 7: Sharon Lee (Ypsilanti Community Schools), Michael McVey (Saline Area Schools), Jack Temsey (Eaton RESA), Mary Vincent (Monroe Public Schools), and Dale Wingerd (Clinton Community Schools, Lenawee County).
- Region 8, Troy's region: Melandie Hines (Wayne-Westland Community Schools, Wayne County), Birgit McQuiston (Lake Orion Community Schools, Oakland County), and Evelyn Pridemore (Redford Union School District, Wayne County).

Voting procedure. Each member district received one ballot, emailed to the superintendent's secretary of record with MASB on January 26, 2024. No local district or ISD funds may be used to campaign for any candidate. The booklet notes that incumbents appear in bold and directs readers to candidate statements on the following pages. For Troy, the practical decision was selecting among the three Region 8 candidates.

A presentation titled 'Recommendations for Schools of Choice, 2024-2025 School Year,' prepared by Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, and delivered at the Troy Board of Education's February 6, 2024 workshop; it closes with a decision memo dated Tuesday, February 27, 2024 addressed to the Board.

Program background. Schools of Choice provides non-resident students additional enrollment opportunities; participation is optional for districts, and the degree of participation - application/enrollment dates, grade levels, and building assignment - is set locally. Elementary enrollment projections were submitted by Plante Moran Cresa, with kindergarten and first-grade 'most likely' versus 'actual' figures shown for 2021/2022 through 2024/2025 (for example, 2023/2024 kindergarten most-likely 777 versus actual 817).

2023-2024 elementary SOC data. The district enrolled 188 elementary SOC students against 4,897 non-SOC students, an overall SOC rate of 3.70%. By building, Hill Elementary had by far the highest SOC concentration at 17.14% (60 SOC/290 non-SOC), followed by Wass at 7.85% (34), Wattles at 5.37% (22), Costello at 4.43% (18), Leonard 2.92% (12), Hamilton 2.87% (13), Barnard 2.35% (10), Troy Union 2.23% (9), Martell 1.88% (7), Morse 0.48% (2), and Bemis 0.22% (1); Schroeder Elementary, the TSD Preschool, and VLAC had zero SOC students. By grade level the 188 SOC students were: 15 kindergarten (2.06%), 22 first (2.61%), 38 second (4.78%), 39 third (4.60%), 34 fourth (3.96%), and 40 fifth (4.33%). By ethnicity, SOC students were 61.70% White (116), with 30 Asian (15.96%), 18 Black (9.57%), 14 multi-ethnic, and 10 Hispanic - a notably different mix than the non-SOC population, which was 43.03% White and 40.13% Asian. Among subgroups, SOC students included 27 English learners, 48 Free/Reduced Lunch, and 24 Special Education.

Districtwide enrollment context. A separate table lists non-SOC students by grade for 2023-2024 totaling 11,466 across K-12 (for example, kindergarten 802 and twelfth grade 1,008), alongside a kindergarten/first-grade history running from 2009-2010 through 2023-2024.

Sibling-preference projection. A survey emailed to current SOC families identified students eligible under sibling preference for 2024-2025: 11 kindergarten, 1 first grade, and 7 middle school (2 sixth-grade, 4 seventh-grade, 1 eighth-grade).

Recommendation. The concluding memo recommends using Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his formula (most likely plus low, divided by 2) as the basis for determining how many SOC students to admit, and accepting SOC applications for 100 Kindergarten and 30 First Grade students. (Portions of the memo's narrative retain template language referencing the 2016-2017 and 2015-2016 school years.) The document's purpose is to give the Board the enrollment analysis and admission-cap recommendation needed to authorize the 2024-2025 Schools of Choice program.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Restorative Practices (RP) board overview presentation given on February 6, 2024 at a Troy Board of Education workshop. The stated learning intentions were to gain knowledge of RP principles, learn ways to enact RP in school environments, and discover how implementation affects social change, with outcomes of explaining the RP model, engaging in reflective thinking, and applying RP principles.

Presenters: Casey Conaton, Assistant Principal at Smith Middle School, whose experience includes Foundations in Restorative Practice (2012) via Macomb County Intermediate School District training from The Resolution Center and Train-the-Trainer, Restorative Practices (2022) through Troy School District training from IIRP trainer Bill Boyle; and Chantelle Yancy, Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion & Community Relations, whose experience includes Restorative Justice Training (2010) from Marygrove College's Social Justice Program and Foundations in Restorative Practices (2023) from Rochester Community Schools.

The presentation defines restorative practices, citing the International Institute for Restorative Practices (iirp.edu), as a field within the social sciences that studies how to strengthen relationships between individuals and social connections within communities; a continuum of proactive components supporting strong relationships and safe communities where all members feel they belong; and accountability focused on repairing harm and learning from mistakes. The RP framework is presented as "Fair Process: Do with, not to," comprising Engagement (engaging with the individual, sharing concerns and problem-solving), Explanation (explaining why the parties are there), and Expectation Clarity (ensuring the outcome and expectations are clearly understood). A Restorative Practices Continuum and seven factors to consider are referenced.

On the rationale, schools adopt RP as a comprehensive way to address disparities in exclusionary discipline such as suspensions and expulsions, using proactive, preventative approaches; conflict is addressed through community for repair rather than only two individuals, and restorative justice provides an alternative accountability process ensuring those harmed are heard and are active participants.

Applying RP to student discipline, the presentation ties it to the TSD Student Code of Conduct. Restorative discipline focuses on the harms, needs, and causes of student behavior rather than only rule-breaking and punishment, giving students opportunities to be accountable and repair harm. Student violators may engage in restorative practices as a consequence, provided they freely admit wrongdoing and express contrition. Listed activities include restitution; alternative suspension including In-School Suspension/Detention; written and verbal apology; participation in diversion programs; community service; outreach and awareness activities; a course of study, book study, or applied learning experience; a behavior plan or behavior contract; counseling in and out of school; agency and community supports; and student-to-student mediation.

Examples of RP in a school setting include Suite360 modules used for discipline and restorative measures before more severe consequences, peer conflict resolution, reflective questioning (what happened, what were you thinking, what have you thought about since), re-entry meetings after major discipline, student/teacher conflict resolution using restorative questions, and teachers establishing classroom community circles. The presentation also addresses misconceptions, including the beliefs that RP does not hold students accountable and that teachers should only focus on academics.

Building-level SOC counts and shares include Hill Elementary 60 (17.14%), Wass Elementary 34 (7.85%), Wattles Elementary 22 (5.37%), Costello Elementary 18 (4.43%), Hamilton Elementary 13, Leonard Elementary 12, Barnard Elementary 10, Troy Union Elementary 9, Martell Elementary 7, Morse Elementary 2, Bemis Elementary 1, and Schroeder Elementary 0. SOC students by grade included Kindergarten 15, First 22, Second 38, Third 39, Fourth 34, and Fifth 40. This Operations Department memorandum, dated March 5, 2024, was sent by Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, to Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, regarding RFP 2324-04 - Site Work - Retention Pond Project. The department is located at 1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083 (phone 248.823.4050, fax 248.823.4077). The memo reports that an issue identified at Athens High School regarding the retention pond restoration was producing costs exceeding the project contingency amount.

The district was performing retention pond restoration work at Athens High, Baker Middle, and Leonard Elementary Schools during the winter/spring, with a bid cost of $356,800.00 and a 7% contingency of $24,976.00, for a total project award of $381,776.00. The specific problem concerned the large retention pond running parallel to the South service drive at Athens, which was heavily concentrated with phragmites, trees, and other vegetation. The original soil removal estimate had been based on samples and experienced forecasted quantities provided by PEA Engineering. After the growth was removed and the soils exposed, the amount of excavation, removal, and reestablishment needed proved greater than the bid scope.

Site meetings and discussions were held to evaluate the appropriate quantities and project costs. Approximately 1,200 yards of unsuitable soil needed to be hauled off and the same amount imported to reestablish the pond. The district was able to identify that soil being removed from the Athens Auxiliary Soccer Field would meet the desired quantity and quality, which left the excavation and removal costs as an additional expense not covered by the base bid. Eagle Excavation estimated a cost of $73,000.00 for the additional removal and disposal of the unsuitable soils, an amount PEA evaluated and concurred with.

Carson noted that the Leonard portion of the project was complete and the Baker portion substantially complete, with only some removal and restoration remaining; neither had required contingency funds, leaving the $24,976.00 contingency intact. On that basis, he requested an additional $50,000.00 in funding from the Building Site & Sinking Fund to properly complete the Athens portion of the Retention Pond Restoration Project.

Resolution
Certifies the district's non-homestead Operating Millage Renewal Proposal to the Oakland County Clerk (School District Election Coordinator) for submission to voters at the August 6, 2024 election, with certification due by 4:00 p.m. on May 14, 2024.

Exhibit A - proposal terms
- Renews authority to levy up to 18.00 mills for general school district operating purposes on non-exempt taxable property.
- Protects against Headlee rollbacks of up to 4.0 mills; increases the tax limitation to 22 mills, with 18 mills the maximum allowable levy ($18.00 per $1,000 of taxable value).
- Restricts the levy on principal residences (owner-occupied homes) to no more than 5.7313 mills.
- Applies to non-homestead property (principally industrial and commercial real property and residential rental property); the current authority expires with the district's 2025 tax levy.
- Term: twenty (20) years, the years 2026 to 2045 inclusive.
- The first-year revenue amount is left blank in the draft.

Purpose
Place the operating millage renewal before Troy voters so the district can continue to receive its full per-pupil foundation allowance.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This version of business item 8.A pairs the Troy School District's Resolution Certifying the Operating Millage Renewal Proposal with the full text of Exhibit A, the ballot proposal itself. The resolution is drafted as minutes of a regular Board of Education meeting to be held April 16, 2024 at 7:00 p.m., with blank fields for present and absent members and for the offering and supporting members. Its recitals mirror the companion resolution: the Board has determined it is necessary for continuing operation of the district to renew authority to levy certain operating mills described in the attached Proposal; it is necessary and desirable to submit the Proposal to electors at an election on August 6, 2024; and the Proposal must be certified to the Clerk of Oakland County (the School District Election Coordinator) no later than 4:00 p.m. on May 14, 2024. The operative clauses certify the Proposal for submission, authorize the Secretary and Superintendent to file it and to update it for any 2024 Headlee rollbacks, direct the Election Coordinator to post and publish notices and print ballots in the form of Exhibit A, and rescind conflicting resolutions. It is signed and certified by Gary Hauff, Secretary of the Board of Education, referencing the Open Meetings Act (Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976).

Exhibit A sets out the Operating Millage Renewal Proposal. As explained in the narrative, the proposal would renew the district's authority to levy up to 18.00 mills for general school district operating purposes on taxable property not exempt from the levy, protect the district against the impact of Headlee rollbacks of up to 4.0 mills, and restrict the levy on principal residences (owner-occupied homes) to no more than 5.7313 mills. The authorization would allow the district to continue levying the statutory limit of 18.00 mills on non-homestead property (principally industrial and commercial real property and residential rental property), authority that expires with the district's 2025 tax levy. Under existing law the district would levy on principal-residence property only the portion of mills necessary to receive the full revenue per-pupil foundation allowance permitted by the State.

The ballot question asks whether the limitation on the amount of taxes that may be imposed on taxable property in the Troy School District, County of Oakland, Michigan, be increased to 22 mills, with 18 mills being the maximum allowable levy ($18.00 per $1,000 of taxable value), to the extent such property is not statutorily exempt, and of which not more than 5.7313 mills may be imposed on principal residences, for twenty (20) years, the years 2026 to 2045 inclusive, to provide funds for operating expenses of the School District. The proposal states the millage would raise approximately a dollar figure left blank in the draft in the first year of levy, followed by YES and NO ballot options.

Historical operating millage
- Sourced from the Oakland Equalization Department and district historical L-4029 forms.

Headlee impact modeling
- Estimates the reduction in state aid from projected Headlee Millage Reduction Fraction (MRF) rollbacks over 20 years, at a 4-mill buffer (MRF 0.9900 and 0.9882) and a 5-mill buffer (MRF 0.9882).
- Assumptions: estimated 2023 equivalent non-PRE taxable value of $1,722,654,355; annual non-PRE taxable value growth of 5% in 2024 and 2% thereafter; constant MRFs; excludes the Hold Harmless millage.

Estimated cumulative loss in state aid over 20 years
- 4-mill buffer at 0.9900 rollback: $526,140.
- 4-mill buffer at 0.9882 rollback: $5,902,057.
- 5-mill buffer at 0.9882 rollback: $204,424.

Purpose
Inform the Board's choice of Headlee buffer for the operating millage renewal proposal.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Prepared by PFM Financial Advisors LLC of Ann Arbor, Michigan (555 Briarwood Circle, Suite 333, Ann Arbor 48108; office 734-994-9700; Pfm.com) and dated February 20, 2024, this analysis examines the Troy School District's non-homestead operating tax millage rate in support of business item 8.A, the operating millage renewal proposal.

The report first presents the district's historical operating millage, sourced from the Oakland Equalization Department and the district's historical L-4029 forms. The table covers levy years 2004 through 2023 and shows that the district levied a total of 18.0000 mills in nearly every year, split between an operating millage levied component and a hedge millage component. For 2023, the operating millage levied was 16.9612 and the hedge millage 1.0388, totaling 18.0000. The table also reports average total-millage reduction fractions of 0.9882 over 5 years, 0.9916 over 10 years, 0.9944 over 15 years, and 0.9958 over 20 years, illustrating the modest historical effect of Headlee rollbacks.

The core of the analysis is an Example Headlee Impact estimating the reduction in state aid due to the projected impact of Headlee Millage Reduction Fraction (MRF) rollbacks on the district's non-PRE operating millage revenues. It models a 4-mill buffer using MRFs of 0.9900 and 0.9882 (the 5-year average) and a 5-mill buffer using an MRF of 0.9882, each over a 20-year horizon covering levy years 2026 through 2045. Key assumptions include an estimated 2023 equivalent non-PRE taxable value of $1,722,654,355; annual growth in non-PRE taxable value of 5% in 2024 and 2% thereafter; constant Headlee rollback MRFs as noted (with a caveat that actual MRFs will vary each year); and exclusion of any effect on the Hold Harmless millage.

Under these assumptions, the estimated cumulative loss in annual state aid funding over the 20 years is $526,140 at a 4-mill buffer with a 0.9900 rollback; $5,902,057 at a 4-mill buffer with a 0.9882 rollback; and $204,424 at a 5-mill buffer with a 0.9882 rollback. In each scenario the modeled losses are zero in the early years and appear only toward the end of the period. For example, under the 4-mill buffer at 0.9882 the annual loss grows from $51,133 in 2041 (levy year 16) to $600,253 in 2042, $1,164,721 in 2043, $1,744,877 in 2044, and $2,341,072 in 2045.

A detailed year-by-year calculation table follows, showing for each levy year the non-homestead taxable value (rising from $1,722,654,355 in 2023 toward roughly $2.6 billion by 2043 under the growth assumptions), the prior-year and current Headlee factors and millage rates, the buffer, and the resulting estimated revenue loss at the equivalent non-PRE taxable value. The tables are presented for informational purposes only and are intended to help the Board weigh how large a Headlee buffer (4 versus 5 mills) to build into the operating millage renewal proposal it places before voters.

This document is the Troy School District "Mission Moment" recognition and accompanying resolution for agenda item 2.B. at the regular Board of Education meeting on April 16, 2024, tied to Autism Acceptance Month.

April is designated as Autism Acceptance Month, and the document states that the Troy School District recognizes the need for public awareness to promote acceptance, celebrate differences, and be more inclusive toward autistic individuals. In honor of the month, the Board intends to pass a resolution celebrating the contributions of neurodiverse people and working toward ending disparities. Before adopting the resolution, the Board recognizes the team at Morse Elementary School for its Morse Friendship Cookies Peer to Peer Program. Morse Principal Scott Keen is present to share more about the program, introduce his team, and show a short video. The recommended action is to invite Mr. Keen to introduce his team and distribute certificates to team members, then read and adopt the resolution; the document includes blank "Moved by" and "Supported by" lines.

The resolution's recitals state: that Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States; that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report that 1 in 36 children may have autism; that autism is a neurological and developmental disorder characterized by social impairment and restricted interactive and communication behaviors, and can affect anyone regardless of race, ethnicity, gender, or socioeconomic background; that symptoms and characteristics may present in a variety of combinations and can result in significant, lifelong challenges in areas affecting learning, daily living, employment, social-interactive behaviors, and understanding verbal and nonverbal communication; that as efforts continue, physicians, psychologists, behavior analysts, speech and language pathologists, occupational therapists, vocational rehabilitation professionals, and educators can assist persons with autism and their families by supporting early identification, education, intervention, recreation, and other opportunities vital to enhanced development and well-being; and that the Troy School District is honored to celebrate the many ways individuals with autism enhance the school community and is committed to fostering acceptance and belonging.

The operative clause resolves that the Board of Education hereby recognizes April 2024 as Autism Acceptance Month in the Troy School District. The document ends with blank "Yes" and "No" lines for recording the Board's vote.

This memorandum, dated May 1, 2024, is from Gayle Moran, Food Service Liaison, to Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, regarding 'Wass Elementary Equipment Purchases for Spend Down Plan.'

Moran explains that the district currently has an excess of funds in its Food Service Account, an amount determined by the Michigan Department of Education (MDE). The district will use these excess funds to improve and/or replace equipment within the Food Service Department. The specific recommendation in this memo is to replace the ovens at Wass Elementary with equipment previously approved by MDE.

Because the equipment involved consists entirely of portable items, the purchase was competitively bid. Bids were received and opened on May 2, 2024, and a bid tabulation was included with the memo (the tabulation table itself is not rendered in the extracted text). Based on the bid results, Moran recommends awarding the bid to Gold Star Products for $32,542.00 as the lowest responsible bidder.

The formal recommendation is to award the purchase of two electric combi ovens to Gold Star Products, Inc. for $32,542.00. Moran notes that a copy of the Request for Proposal (RFP) and the bids are included with the memo for review. The purchase will be funded by the Food Service Fund as part of the district's excess fund balance spend-down plan, and Moran emphasizes that the items are on the approved replacement list with the Michigan Department of Education.

The companion quote packet for this procurement (the Wass Oven Quotes document) details the equipment specification -- UNOX USA ChefTop MIND.Maps Plus electric combi ovens configured as two ovens in one double stack -- and records a bid of $36,457.91 from Great Lakes Hotel Supply of Southfield, Michigan, a higher price than the recommended Gold Star Products award of $32,542.00. The purpose of this memo is to obtain approval to complete the oven replacement at Wass Elementary using excess food-service funds, consistent with MDE's spend-down expectations and approved-equipment list.
